name: Wari Empire
summary: An Andean state centred near Ayacucho, Peru, often seen as an early empire before the Inca. It built planned administrative centres and roads.

location.value: Emerged in Peru’s Ayacucho Basin and spread its influence over much of the Peruvian highlands and coast.

terrain.value: Highland valleys and steep mountainsides turned into farmland with terraces.
terrain.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

climate.value: Highland climate with wet and dry seasons; a long drought may have contributed to its decline.
climate.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

resources.value: Terraced fields of maize and potatoes, llama and alpaca herds, and obsidian.
resources.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

disasters.value: Drought around the end of the first millennium.
disasters.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

population.value: No reliable estimate; the capital may have held tens of thousands.
population.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

urbanisation.value: The capital Huari covered several square kilometres of walled compounds.
urbanisation.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

disease.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

migration.value: Colonists and officials were sent to new provincial centres.
migration.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

economicBase.value: Terraced, irrigated farming and herding, with state-organised labour.
economicBase.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

tradeRoutes.value: A network of roads, many later reused by the Inca.
tradeRoutes.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.
wealth.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

moneyAndTax.value: No coinage; the state probably collected labour service, as the Inca later did.
moneyAndTax.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

inequality.value: Rich elite tombs and palaces show a powerful ruling class.
inequality.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

governmentType.value: An expansionist state, often described as the first Andean empire.
governmentType.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

keyRulers.value: No rulers are known by name; there was no writing.
keyRulers.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

succession.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

institutions.value: Planned administrative centres such as Pikillacta and Viracochapampa.
institutions.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

stability.source: Wikipedia: Wari Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

eliteConflict.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

armyAndTech.value: Little is known; warrior images appear on pottery.
armyAndTech.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

majorWars.value: No specific wars are known, though its spread may have involved conquest.
majorWars.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

territoryChange.value: Expanded across much of Peru by about 800.
territoryChange.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

alliancesRivals.value: Tiwanaku was a contemporary; Wari was once thought to derive from it.

inventions.value: Large-scale agricultural terraces and early road systems.
inventions.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

scienceEducation.value: Early khipu (knotted cords) were used to keep records.
scienceEducation.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

openness.value: Shared religious imagery, such as the Staff God, with Tiwanaku.
openness.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

religion.value: Worship of the Staff God, shared with Tiwanaku.
religion.source: Wikipedia: Wari Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

languageWriting.value: Unknown; Aymara or an early form of Quechua have been suggested.

artsArchitecture.value: Fine tapestry tunics and large painted ceramic urns.
artsArchitecture.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

socialStructure.value: Rulers and officials, specialists (weavers, potters), farmers.
socialStructure.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

sharedIdentity.value: A shared state religion and pottery style.
sharedIdentity.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

neighbours.value: Tiwanaku, and the regions of the earlier Moche and Nazca.
neighbours.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

ideasReligions.value: Spread the Staff God imagery across the Andes.
ideasReligions.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

colonisation.value: Established provincial centres far from the capital.
colonisation.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

riseSignals.value: Emerged around 600 CE in the Ayacucho Basin.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Wari Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

peakPeriod.value: Around the 8th–9th centuries, with administrative centres across Peru.
peakPeriod.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

declineSignals.source: Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

outcome.value: Ended by about 1100; local kingdoms followed, and later the Inca.

overallCertainty.value: Low to medium. With no writing, its government is inferred from archaeology.

knownFor.label: Wari tapestry tunics
knownFor.note: Very finely woven tunics with bold geometric designs.

knownFor.label: Early khipu
knownFor.note: Knotted-cord records, later used by the Inca.

knownFor.label: Pikillacta
knownFor.note: A planned administrative centre near Cusco.
